claim: Information processing by cerebellar molecular layer interneurons (MLIs) plays a crucial role in motor behavior.
source: Information processing by cerebellar molecular layer interneurons (MLIs) plays a crucial role in motor behavior.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about cerebellar function.

claim: MLI recruitment is tightly controlled by the profile of short-term plasticity (STP) at granule cell (GC)-MLI synapses.
source: MLI recruitment is tightly controlled by the profile of short-term plasticity (STP) at granule cell (GC)-MLI synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings presented in the manuscript, particularly the data showing correlation between STP profiles and MLI firing patterns.

claim: GCs are the most numerous neurons in the brain.
source: While GCs are the most numerous neurons in the brain, STP diversity at GC-MLI synapses is poorly documented.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in neuroscience literature.

claim: STP diversity at GC-MLI synapses is poorly documented.
source: While GCs are the most numerous neurons in the brain, STP diversity at GC-MLI synapses is poorly documented.
evidence: This claim is based on a review of existing literature and identifies a gap in knowledge.

claim: Four classes of connections at GC-MLI synapses are segregated by their STP profile.
source: Using slice recordings at individual GC-MLI synapses of mice, we revealed four classes of connections segregated by their STP profile.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the PCA and k-means clustering analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Each class of GC-MLI connection differentially drives MLI recruitment.
source: Each class differentially drives MLI recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by the photostimulation experiments showing different delays to frequency peak for different connection classes (Figure 7).

claim: GC synaptic diversity is underlain by heterogeneous expression of synapsin II.
source: We show that GC synaptic diversity is underlain by heterogeneous expression of synapsin II, a key actor of STP
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry and electron microscopy data showing variable Syn II expression (Figure 4).

claim: Synapsin II is a key actor of STP.
source: We show that GC synaptic diversity is underlain by heterogeneous expression of synapsin II, a key actor of STP
evidence: This is supported by both literature citations and the functional studies in Syn II KO mice.

claim: GC terminals devoid of synapsin II are associated with slow MLI recruitment.
source: that GC terminals devoid of synapsin II are associated with slow MLI recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by the increased delay to first spike in Syn II KO mice (Figure 8).

claim: Molecular, structural and functional diversity across GC terminals provides a mechanism to expand the coding range of MLIs.
source: Our study reveals that molecular, structural and functional diversity across GC terminals provides a mechanism to expand the coding range of MLIs.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the integration of all experimental findings.

claim: Inhibitory interneurons mediating feed-back or feed-forward inhibition (FFI) provide brain microcircuits with an exquisite temporal control over the firing frequency of projecting neurons.
source: Inhibitory interneurons mediating feed-back or feed-forward inhibition (FFI) provide brain microcircuits with an exquisite temporal control over the firing frequency of projecting neurons (Hennequin et al., 2017; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Klausberger and Somogyi, 2008; O'Donnell et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: In the cerebellar cortex, the FFI microcircuit is activated by granule cells (GCs) that target two types of molecular layer interneurons (MLIs): stellate cells (SCs) and basket cells (BCs).
source: In the cerebellar cortex, the FFI microcircuit is activated by granule cells (GCs) that target two types of molecular layer interneurons (MLIs): stellate cells (SCs) and basket cells (BCs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar anatomy and circuitry.

claim: SCs and BCs control Purkinje cells (PC), the sole projecting neurons of the cerebellar cortex, through a powerful somatic or dendritic inhibition.
source: SCs and BCs finally control Purkinje cells (PC), the sole projecting neurons of the cerebellar cortex, through a powerful somatic or dendritic inhibition (Jörntell et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The FFI encodes sensorimotor information through acceleration or deceleration of PC simple spike activity.
source: In combination with the direct excitatory pathway provided by GC-PC connections, the FFI encodes sensorimotor information through acceleration or deceleration of PC simple spike activity (Armstrong and Edgley, 1988; Jelitai et al., 2016; Ozden et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Sensorimotor information is conveyed to the cerebellar cortex by mossy fibers (MFs) as short high-frequency bursts of action potentials.
source: Sensorimotor information is conveyed to the cerebellar cortex by mossy fibers (MFs) as short high-frequency bursts of action potentials (Chadderton et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2017; Jörntell and Ekerot, 2006; Kennedy et al., 2014; Powell et al., 2015; Rancz et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: During high-frequency stimulations, cerebellar synapses exhibit several forms of short-term synaptic plasticity (STP) including facilitation and depression of synaptic responses in the millisecond range.
source: During high-frequency stimulations, cerebellar synapses exhibit several forms of short-term synaptic plasticity (STP) including facilitation and depression of synaptic responses in the millisecond range (Atluri and Regehr, 1996; Bao et al., 2010; Brachtendorf et al., 2015; Dittman et al., 2000; Doussau et al., 2017; Miki et al., 2016; Valera et al., 2012; Zheng and Raman, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: STP play multiple roles in information processing.
source: STP play multiple roles in information processing (Anwar et al., 2017; Fioravante and Regehr, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Heterogeneity of STP across MF-GC synapses provides a mechanism for coding multisensory events at the level of single GCs.
source: At the input stage of the cerebellar cortex, a strategy based on the heterogeneity of STP across MF-GC synapses provides a mechanism for coding multisensory events at the level of single GCs (Chabrol et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Differences in the profile of STP across synapses involved in the direct excitatory pathway or in the FFI microcircuit control the inhibitory/excitatory balance and shape Purkinje cell discharge.
source: Also, differences in the profile of STP across synapses involved in the direct excitatory pathway or in the FFI microcircuit control the inhibitory/excitatory balance and shape Purkinje cell discharge (Grangeray-Vilmint et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: GCs segregate in clonally related subpopulations.
source: GCs which are the most numerous neurons in the brain, segregate in clonally related subpopulations (Espinosa and Luo, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The behavior of glutamate release during high-frequency activities at GC boutons is determined by the target cell.
source: A seminal study has shown that the behavior of glutamate release during high-frequency activities at GC boutons is determined by the target cell (that is PC, SC or BC, Bao et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: GC-BC synapses depress during high-frequency stimulation while GC-SC synapses facilitate.
source: Following compound stimulations of clusters of GCs or beams of parallel fibers (PFs), it was shown that GC-BC synapses depress during high-frequency stimulation while GC-SC synapses facilitate (Bao et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Target cell–dependency of STP at the input stage of the FFI pathway has important functional consequences for cerebellar output.
source: By controlling the spatiotemporal excitability of PC (Bao et al., 2010), and potentially by shaping the inhibitory/excitatory balance (Grangeray-Vilmint et al., 2018), target cell–dependency of STP at the input stage of the FFI pathway must have important functional consequences for cerebellar output.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited studies and logical reasoning.

claim: Many MLIs cannot be classified solely by their axon profile or their position in the molecular layer.
source: However, target cell–dependency of STP at GC-MLI synapses is challenged by different experimental findings. First, many MLIs cannot be classified solely by their axon profile (e.g. basket versus dendritic synapses) or their position in the molecular layer (Palay and Chan-Palay, 1974; Sultan and Bower, 1998)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MLIs represent a single population of interneurons.
source: and it was proposed that MLIs represent a single population of interneurons (Jörntell et al., 2010; Rakic, 1972; Sotelo, 2015; Sultan and Bower, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Release properties and STP profiles of GC synaptic inputs to MLIs can be modified by presynaptic long-term plasticity and by local retrograde signaling independently of the target cell.
source: Second, release properties and STP profiles of GC synaptic inputs to MLIs can be modified by presynaptic long-term plasticity and by local retrograde signaling independently of the target cell (Bender et al., 2009; Soler-Llavina and Sabatini, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Synapsins (Syn) are good candidates underlying functional heterogeneity across cerebellar synapses.
source: Among presynaptic proteins involved in STP, synapsins (Syn) are good candidates underlying functional heterogeneity across cerebellar synapses.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on knowledge of synapsin function.

claim: Syn are presynaptic phosphoproteins coded by three distinct genes (Syn I, II and III).
source: Syn are presynaptic phosphoproteins coded by three distinct genes (Syn I, II and III).
evidence: This is established knowledge about synapsin molecular biology.

claim: Both Syn I and Syn II regulate neurotransmitter release and STP in mature synapses.
source: Both Syn I and Syn II regulate neurotransmitter release and STP in mature synapses (Cesca et al., 2010; Humeau et al., 2011; Song and Augustine, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The synapse-specific expression of Syn isoforms contributes to the diversity of STP profiles.
source: The synapse-specific expression of Syn isoforms (Bragina et al., 2010; Patton et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2011) contributes to the diversity of STP profiles (Feliciano et al., 2017; Gitler et al., 2004; Kielland et al., 2006; Song and Augustine, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Synapsin expression determines the inhibitory-excitatory balance in cortical and hippocampal networks.
source: and determines the inhibitory-excitatory balance in cortical and hippocampal networks (Fassio et al., 2011; Ketzef and Gitler, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MLIs, regardless of their identity, receive four functionally distinct types of synapses from GCs.
source: Here, we show that MLIs, regardless of their identity, receive four functionally distinct types of synapses from GCs.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing four classes of connections in both SCs and BCs (Figures 2 and 3).

claim: Differences in STP across GC-MLI connections are underlain by heterogeneous expression of Syn II at GC-MLI synapses.
source: Differences in STP across GC-MLI connections are underlain by heterogeneous expression of Syn II at GC-MLI synapses.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry, electron microscopy, and functional studies in Syn II KO mice (Figures 4, 5, 6).

claim: Syn II determines the profile of STP and the first-spike latency in MLI.
source: Functional studies using wild-type (WT) and Syn II knockout (KO) mice demonstrate that Syn II determines the profile of STP and the first-spike latency in MLI.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of STP profiles and firing patterns between WT and Syn II KO mice (Figures 5 and 8).

claim: Single MLIs receive GC inputs with distinct molecular and functional properties.
source: Our observation that single MLIs receive GC inputs with distinct molecular and functional properties suggests that the temporal coding of GC activity by MLIs and thereby the inhibitory control over the cerebellar output via PCs depends on GC subtypes recruited by a given sensorimotor input.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data showing multiple classes of inputs to individual MLIs (Figure 1).

claim: The temporal coding of GC activity by MLIs depends on GC subtypes recruited by a given sensorimotor input.
source: Our observation that single MLIs receive GC inputs with distinct molecular and functional properties suggests that the temporal coding of GC activity by MLIs and thereby the inhibitory control over the cerebellar output via PCs depends on GC subtypes recruited by a given sensorimotor input.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: STP profiles were highly heterogeneous across unitary GC-MLI contacts.
source: STP profiles were highly heterogeneous across unitary GC-MLI contacts (n = 96) including unitary connections contacting the same MLI (Figure 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) followed by k-means clustering analysis identified four clusters that characterize STP at GC-MLI synapses.
source: To classify the STP profiles, we used principal component analysis (PCA) on the averaged and normalized synaptic charges in trains of EPSCs followed by a k-means clustering analysis (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2). We identified four clusters that characterize STP at GC-MLI synapses (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by the PCA and clustering analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The four STP profile classes differ by the quantity of neurotransmitter released at the first stimuli.
source: The profiles differ by: (i) the quantity of neurotransmitter released at the first stimuli (Figure 2C, left)
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The four STP profile classes differ by paired-pulse plasticity.
source: The profiles differ by: (i) the quantity of neurotransmitter released at the first stimuli (Figure 2C, left), (ii) paired-pulse plasticity (Figure 2C, right)
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The four STP profile classes differ by the STP profiles during the first four EPSCs.
source: The profiles differ by: (i) the quantity of neurotransmitter released at the first stimuli (Figure 2C, left), (ii) paired-pulse plasticity (Figure 2C, right), (iii) the STP profiles during the first four EPSCs
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The four STP profile classes differ by the ability to sustain glutamate release after the fourth stimuli.
source: The profiles differ by: (i) the quantity of neurotransmitter released at the first stimuli (Figure 2C, left), (ii) paired-pulse plasticity (Figure 2C, right), (iii) the STP profiles during the first four EPSCs, and (iv) the ability to sustain glutamate release after the fourth stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The profile of STP was conserved during 10 successive 100 Hz trains.
source: We checked whether the profile of STP was conserved during 10 successive 100 Hz trains. The systematic narrow clustering of 10 recordings belonging to the same series of stimulations in the cloud of point of PCA transformation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B) clearly indicated that the profiles of STP were conserved from one train to another during successive stimulations of the same synaptic contact.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a lack of correlation between the charge of the first EPSCs and the stimulation current intensity.
source: However, the lack of correlation between the charge of the first EPSCs, PPR, PC1 or PC2 and the stimulation current intensity indicated that STP profiles were not affected by this parameter (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The classification of inputs using PCA transformation followed by k-mean clustering analysis was weakly affected when EPSCs at the first stimulus were excluded from the dataset.
source: However, the classification of inputs using PCA transformation followed by k-mean clustering analysis was weakly affected when EPSCs at the first stimulus were excluded from the dataset (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Only C1 connections exhibited depression of glutamate release after the second pulse.
source: Among the four groups identified, only C1 connections exhibited depression of glutamate release after the second pulse, while C2 and C3 connections exhibited facilitation (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: C2 and C3 connections exhibited facilitation.
source: Among the four groups identified, only C1 connections exhibited depression of glutamate release after the second pulse, while C2 and C3 connections exhibited facilitation (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: C2 and C3 connections differed in their responses after the fourth stimulus.
source: C2 and C3 connections differed in their responses after the fourth stimulus: while C3 connections sustained release during the entire train, synaptic transmission at C2 connections depressed after the fourth stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: C3 connections sustained release during the entire train.
source: C2 and C3 connections differed in their responses after the fourth stimulus: while C3 connections sustained release during the entire train, synaptic transmission at C2 connections depressed after the fourth stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Synaptic transmission at C2 connections depressed after the fourth stimuli.
source: C2 and C3 connections differed in their responses after the fourth stimulus: while C3 connections sustained release during the entire train, synaptic transmission at C2 connections depressed after the fourth stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: C4 connections were characterized by small but stable EPSCs.
source: On the other hand, C4 connections were characterized by small but stable EPSCs (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: C4 connections correspond to boutons releasing one quanta per stimulation.
source: On the other hand, C4 connections were characterized by small but stable EPSCs (Figure 2C) suggesting that they correspond to boutons releasing one quanta per stimulation (Bender et al., 2009; Nahir and Jahr, 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both MLI subtypes (BCs and SCs) were contacted by functionally distinct GC inputs.
source: Both MLI subtypes were contacted by functionally distinct GC inputs.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: All classes of GC inputs except C3 connections were found on both SCs and BCs.
source: Except for C3 connections (facilitating profiles) absent in BCs, all classes of GC inputs were found on SCs and BCs (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: C3 connections (facilitating profiles) are absent in BCs.
source: Except for C3 connections (facilitating profiles) absent in BCs, all classes of GC inputs were found on SCs and BCs (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The lack of target-cell dependence of STP at GC-MLI synapses was confirmed using compound stimulations of GCs in the granule cell layer.
source: The lack of target-cell dependence of STP at GC-MLI synapses was also confirmed using compound stimulations of GCs in the granule cell layer (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is no correlation between STP profiles and the position of MLIs' soma in the molecular layer.
source: Our analyses failed to establish correlations between STP profiles (evaluated by PC1 or PC2) and the position of MLIs' soma (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) or synaptic inputs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B) in the molecular layer.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There is no correlation between STP profiles and the position of synaptic inputs in the molecular layer.
source: Our analyses failed to establish correlations between STP profiles (evaluated by PC1 or PC2) and the position of MLIs' soma (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) or synaptic inputs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B) in the molecular layer.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: There is no correlation between the distances of excitatory inputs from MLI's soma and STP parameters.
source: Finally, since dendritic integration of excitatory responses in MLI may be influenced by the distance of the synapses from the soma (Tran-Van-Minh et al., 2016) we also checked whether the distances of excitatory inputs from MLI's soma were correlated with STP parameters. Again, our analyses failed to establish a correlation between those parameters (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The different classes of inputs recruited by minimal stimulations were randomly distributed within the molecular layer.
source: Our results indicate that the different classes of inputs recruited by minimal stimulations were randomly distributed within the molecular layer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of correlation between STP profiles and spatial parameters.

claim: Triple staining of cerebellar sections revealed systematic overlap of VGluT1 with Syn I, but not with Syn II.
source: Triple staining of cerebellar sections from P20 ~ P22 CD1 mice (N = 4) revealed systematic overlap of VGluT1 with Syn I, but not with Syn II (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: There is a higher correlation between the fluorescence intensity of Syn I and VGluT1 than between the fluorescence intensity of VGlut1 and Syn II.
source: Quantitative analysis revealed a higher correlation between the fluorescence intensity of Syn I and VGluT1 than between the fluorescence intensity of VGlut1 and Syn II (RSyn I =0.584 +/- 0.057, RSyn II = 0.435 +/- 0.075, paired t-test: p<0.001; n = 52).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Syn I is present in all GC terminals.
source: Our results suggest that Syn I is present in all GC terminals while Syn II is restricted to a subpopulation of GC boutons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Syn II is restricted to a subpopulation of GC boutons.
source: Our results suggest that Syn I is present in all GC terminals while Syn II is restricted to a subpopulation of GC boutons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Immunogold labeling confirmed the ubiquitous presence of Syn I in all GC-MLI synapses.
source: Immunogold labeling confirmed the ubiquitous presence of Syn I in all GC-MLI and presence of Syn II in only 56% of GC terminals contacting MLI (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by the electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Syn II is present in only 56% of GC terminals contacting MLI.
source: Immunogold labeling confirmed the ubiquitous presence of Syn I in all GC-MLI and presence of Syn II in only 56% of GC terminals contacting MLI (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by the electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Absence of Syn II modified the responses of unitary GC-MLI synapses to 100 Hz stimulations.
source: Absence of Syn II modified the responses of unitary GC-MLI synapses to 100 Hz stimulations.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of WT and Syn II KO data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The mean EPSC charges of the first responses was strongly reduced in Syn II KO mice.
source: The mean EPSC charges of the first responses was strongly reduced in Syn II KO mice (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: The percentage of failures at the first stimuli were increased in Syn II KO mice.
source: The percentage of failures at the first stimuli were increased in Syn II KO mice indicating that absence of Syn II decreased the probability of release (pr) of fully-releasable synaptic vesicles (that is, vesicles released by a single action potential, Doussau et al., 2017) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Absence of Syn II decreased the probability of release (pr) of fully-releasable synaptic vesicles.
source: The percentage of failures at the first stimuli were increased in Syn II KO mice indicating that absence of Syn II decreased the probability of release (pr) of fully-releasable synaptic vesicles (that is, vesicles released by a single action potential, Doussau et al., 2017) (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased failure rate and supported by a citation.

claim: The paired-pulse ratio was significantly increased in Syn II KO mice.
source: The paired-pulse ratio was significantly increased in Syn II KO mice (mean/median PPR for WT = 1.1/1.1 ± 0.03, n = 96 and mean/median PPR for Syn II KO mice = 2.6/1.7 ± 0.08, n = 53, p<0.001, MWRST).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of WT and Syn II KO data.

claim: The four profiles of STP found at unitary GC-MLI synapses in WT mice were also found at unitary GC-MLI synapses in Syn II KO mice.
source: The four profiles of STP found at unitary GC-MLI synapses in WT mice were also found at unitary GC-MLI synapses in Syn II KO mice.
evidence: This is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The distribution of the four classes was strongly skewed toward C3 and C4 profiles in Syn II KO mice.
source: However, the distribution of the four classes was strongly skewed toward C3 and C4 profiles (85.8% of the connections, n = 33) in Syn II KO mice (Figure 5E,F)
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: C1 and C2 connections almost disappeared in Syn II KO mice.
source: while C1 and C2 connections almost disappeared (C1 connection 3.6%, C2 connections 10.7%) (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Syn II leads to STP profiles corresponding to C1 and C2.
source: These results suggest Syn II lead to STP profiles corresponding to C1 and C2, whereas GC boutons displaying C3 and C4 profiles are devoid of Syn II.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of WT and Syn II KO data.

claim: GC boutons displaying C3 and C4 profiles are devoid of Syn II.
source: These results suggest Syn II lead to STP profiles corresponding to C1 and C2, whereas GC boutons displaying C3 and C4 profiles are devoid of Syn II.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of WT and Syn II KO data.

claim: The absence of Syn II reduced significantly the number of docked synaptic vesicles at GC-MLI synapses.
source: Morphometric analysis revealed that the absence of Syn II reduced significantly the number of docked synaptic vesicles and the length of the active zone (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is supported by the electron microscopy data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The absence of Syn II reduced significantly the length of the active zone at GC-MLI synapses.
source: Morphometric analysis revealed that the absence of Syn II reduced significantly the number of docked synaptic vesicles and the length of the active zone (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is supported by the electron microscopy data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The absence of Syn II did not affect the positive correlation between the length of the active zone and the number of docked synaptic vesicles.
source: Morphometric analysis revealed that the absence of Syn II reduced significantly the number of docked synaptic vesicles and the length of the active zone (Figure 6B) without affecting the positive correlation between the length of the active zone and the number of docked synaptic (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The presence of Syn II positively regulates the number of docked synaptic vesicles.
source: Altogether, our results suggest that the presence of Syn II positively regulate the number of docked synaptic vesicle and the pr of fully-releasable vesicles, thus enhancing the release glutamate at the onset of burst firing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electron microscopy and functional data.

claim: The presence of Syn II positively regulates the pr of fully-releasable vesicles.
source: Altogether, our results suggest that the presence of Syn II positively regulate the number of docked synaptic vesicle and the pr of fully-releasable vesicles, thus enhancing the release glutamate at the onset of burst firing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data from Syn II KO mice.

claim: Syn II enhances the release of glutamate at the onset of burst firing.
source: Altogether, our results suggest that the presence of Syn II positively regulate the number of docked synaptic vesicle and the pr of fully-releasable vesicles, thus enhancing the release glutamate at the onset of burst firing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined structural and functional data.

claim: The STP profile shapes the spike output pattern of MLIs following compound stimulation of GCs or PFs.
source: The STP profile shapes the spike output pattern of MLIs following compound stimulation of GCs or PFs (Bao et al., 2010; Carter and Regehr, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Each class of GC-MLI synapse should influence the MLI spike output pattern specifically.
source: This suggests that each class of GC-MLI synapse should influence the MLI spike output pattern specifically.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies and the current findings.

claim: Photostimulation of individual GCs increased the MLI firing rate.
source: Photostimulation of individual GCs increased the MLI firing rate confirming that sufficient glutamate was released by unitary GC boutons during high-frequency stimulation to produce spikes in MLIs (Barbour, 1993; Carter and Regehr, 2002) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by the loose-patch recording data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Sufficient glutamate is released by unitary GC boutons during high-frequency stimulation to produce spikes in MLIs.
source: Photostimulation of individual GCs increased the MLI firing rate confirming that sufficient glutamate was released by unitary GC boutons during high-frequency stimulation to produce spikes in MLIs (Barbour, 1993; Carter and Regehr, 2002) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is confirmed by the experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: Photostimulations yielded heterogeneous profile of STP.
source: Photostimulations yielded heterogeneous profile of STP.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7.

claim: PCA followed by k-means clustering analysis revealed three distinct STP profiles (C1', C2' and C3' connections) in photostimulation experiments.
source: PCA followed by k-means clustering analysis revealed three distinct STP profiles (C1', C2' and C3' connections different from C1 to C4 connections since the parameters of bursts elicited in GCs using minimal electrical stimulations and photostimulations are different) that differed by their time course and amplitude (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This is supported by the PCA and clustering analysis shown in Figure 7B-C.

claim: C1' connections are characterized by large responses that peaked at the onset of GC bursts and then rapidly depressed (phasic profile).
source: C1' connections with positive PC1 values were characterized by large responses that peaked at the onset of GC bursts and then rapidly depressed (phasic profile) (averaged EPSC peak charge: −232.8 fC ± 55.2 fC reached at 33.2 ms ± 11.3, n = 14).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis of photostimulation experiments.

claim: C2' connections are characterized by a phasic profile with smaller amplitudes than C1' synapses.
source: C2' connections with low PC1 values were also characterized by a phasic profile, but EPSCs have smaller amplitudes (averaged EPSC peak charge: −121.3 fC ± 21.6 fC reached at 59.7 ms ± 10.3, n = 30) than C1' synapses.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis of photostimulation experiments.

claim: C3' connections are characterized by smaller responses that peaked with longer delays than C1' or C2' synapses.
source: C3' connections were characterized by smaller responses that peaked with longer delays than the ones of C1' or C2' synapses (EPSC peak charge: −133.4 fC ± 21.9 fC reached at 84.4 ms ± 5.4, n = 18).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis of photostimulation experiments.

claim: Stimulation of C1' connections led to faster accelerations of MLI firing rate than stimulation of C2' and C3' connections.
source: Photostimulation of C1' connections accelerated MLI firing rate with a very short delay (<50 ms) compared to C2' and C3' connections (delay > 60 ms) (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: There is a clear relationship between PC1 and the peak frequency.
source: Our analysis also showed a clear relationship between PC1 and the peak frequency (Pearson coefficient, R = 0.7, p=0,008, n = 13).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: A specific STP profile determines the delay to the first spike in MLI in response to GC photostimulation.
source: This indicates that a specific STP profiles determines the delay to the first spike in MLI in response to GC photostimulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation analysis.

claim: The behavior of glutamate release at GC-MLI synapses during high-frequency stimulations is a major determinant of the coding of sensorimotor inputs through the FFI pathway.
source: These results suggest that the behavior of glutamate release at GC-MLI synapses during high-frequency stimulations is a major determinant of the coding of sensorimotor inputs through the FFI pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Identified SCs and BCs both received inputs of different classes upon photostimulation of individual GCs.
source: Similarly to what was observed with minimal stimulation experiments (Figure 3), we found that identified SCs and BCs both received inputs of different classes upon photostimulation of individual GCs (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Genetic deletion of Syn II almost abolished the presence of C1' connections.
source: PCA followed by k-means clustering analysis showed that genetic deletion of Syn II almost abolished the presence of C1' connections and nearly doubled the percentage of C3' connections (Figure 8A–D).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 8A-D.

claim: Genetic deletion of Syn II nearly doubled the percentage of C3' connections.
source: PCA followed by k-means clustering analysis showed that genetic deletion of Syn II almost abolished the presence of C1' connections and nearly doubled the percentage of C3' connections (Figure 8A–D).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 8A-D.

claim: The delay to the first spike significantly increased in Syn II KO mice.
source: Moreover, the delay to the first spike significantly increased in Syn II KO mice (Figure 8E,F), probably due to a lower initial pr at GC-MLI synapses devoid of Syn II (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 8E,F.

claim: The increased delay to first spike in Syn II KO mice is probably due to a lower initial pr at GC-MLI synapses devoid of Syn II.
source: Moreover, the delay to the first spike significantly increased in Syn II KO mice (Figure 8E,F), probably due to a lower initial pr at GC-MLI synapses devoid of Syn II (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data from Figures 5 and 8.

claim: Syn II is a major determinant of burst coding at the GC-MLI synapses.
source: Our results reveal that Syn II is a major determinant of burst coding at the GC-MLI synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined functional studies in WT and Syn II KO mice.

claim: Synapse-specific expression of Syn II diversifies the profile of excitatory drives on MLIs.
source: Synapse-specific expression of Syn II diversifies the profile of excitatory drives on MLIs and expands the coding range in the FFI pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on all the experimental findings.

claim: Synapse-specific expression of Syn II expands the coding range in the FFI pathway.
source: Synapse-specific expression of Syn II diversifies the profile of excitatory drives on MLIs and expands the coding range in the FFI pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on all the experimental findings.

claim: Synaptic efficacy among boutons issued from a single axon varies with the identity of the postsynaptic cell in neocortical or hippocampal circuits.
source: The rules governing diversity in presynaptic release properties have been extensively studied in neocortical or hippocampal circuits. In most of cases, synaptic efficacy among boutons issued from a single axon varies with the identity of the postsynaptic cell (Blackman et al., 2013; Markram et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Target-cell-dependent heterogeneity relies on differences in the probability of release.
source: Target-cell-dependent heterogeneity relies on differences in the probability of release (Koester and Johnston, 2005), responsiveness to neuromodulators (Buchanan et al., 2012; Delaney and Jahr, 2002; Pelkey et al., 2006; Scanziani et al., 1998) or the ability to co-release GABA and glutamate (Galván and Gutiérrez, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The lack of the main facilitating class of input (C3) on BCs may explain why compound GC-BC synaptic responses depress during high-frequency activities.
source: Although the lack of the main facilitating class of input (C3) on BCs may explain why compound GC-BC synaptic responses depress during high-frequency activities, our results argue against target-cell dependency of STP at GC synapses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: The results argue against target-cell dependency of STP at GC synapses.
source: Although the lack of the main facilitating class of input (C3) on BCs may explain why compound GC-BC synaptic responses depress during high-frequency activities, our results argue against target-cell dependency of STP at GC synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings showing heterogeneous inputs to both BCs and SCs.

claim: In compound responses, input classes associated with a strong synaptic strength mask the presence and influence of weak inputs exhibiting other profiles.
source: It is likely that in compound responses, input classes associated with a strong synaptic strength mask the presence and influence of weak inputs exhibiting other profiles.
evidence: This is speculation about why previous studies found target-cell dependency.

claim: The excitatory drive to MLIs and the tuning of the FFI pathway are more complex than expected.
source: Anyhow, our work suggests that the excitatory drive to MLIs and the tuning of the FFI pathway are more complex than expected.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of heterogeneous inputs.

claim: Heterogeneous expression and functions of Syn II in different cell types forming a same neural network have been reported previously.
source: Heterogeneous expression and functions of Syn II in different cell types forming a same neural network have been reported previously (Bragina et al., 2010; Feliciano et al., 2017; Gitler et al., 2004; Kielland et al., 2006; Patton et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: This study brings the first evidence that expression of Syn II at a given connection can be heterogeneous.
source: but our findings bring the first evidence that expression of Syn II at a given connection can be heterogeneous.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Syn II expression may be genetically determined at early developmental stages, leading to Syn II(+) and Syn II(-) subclones of GCs.
source: Syn II expression may be genetically determined at early developmental stages, leading to Syn II(+) and Syn II(-) subclones of GCs.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying Syn II heterogeneity.

claim: Clonally related GCs stack their axons in a specific sub-layer in the molecular layer.
source: It is interesting to note that clonally related GCs (that is, GCs issued from the same GC progenitors) stack their axons in a specific sub-layer in the molecular layer (Espinosa and Luo, 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The presence or absence of Syn II may be organized in a beam-dependent way.
source: suggesting that the presence or absence of Syn II may be organized in a beam-dependent way.
evidence: This is speculation based on the cited study about clonal organization.

claim: Recruitment of Syn II(+) or Syn II(-) connections may be related to the activation of a given sensorimotor task.
source: Since beams of neighboring PFs are activated during sensory stimulations (Wilms and Häusser, 2015), recruitment of Syn II(+) or Syn II(-) connections may be related to the activation of a given sensorimotor task.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of Syn II organization.

claim: Syn II targeting at individual PF boutons may be controlled by mechanisms regulating the traffic of Syn in axons.
source: Alternatively, Syn II targeting at individual PF boutons may be controlled by a complex interplay of mechanisms regulating the traffic of Syn in axons (Gitler et al., 2004) or organizing the assembly of the presynaptic active zone (Owald and Sigrist, 2009).
evidence: This is speculation about alternative mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: Presynaptic diversity arises from parameters that expand the range of synaptic behaviors across GC boutons.
source: Presynaptic diversity also arises from other parameters that probably expand the range of synaptic behaviors across GC boutons.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of synaptic diversity.

claim: Ca2+ dynamics and regulation of Ca2+ influx by neuromodulators in synaptic varicosities from a same PF are highly heterogeneous.
source: Calcium imaging performed on single PFs revealed that Ca2+ dynamics and regulation of Ca2+ influx by neuromodulators in synaptic varicosities from a same PF are highly heterogeneous (Bouvier et al., 2016; Brenowitz and Regehr, 2007; Zhang and Linden, 2009; Zhang and Linden, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Local retrograde release of endocannabinoid by MLI dendrites can affect the functioning of subsets of GC boutons upon sustained activity of PF.
source: Also, local retrograde release of endocannabinoid by MLI dendrites can affect the functioning of subsets of GC boutons upon sustained activity of PF (Beierlein and Regehr, 2006; Soler-Llavina and Sabatini, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Functional heterogeneities among GC terminals originate from the history of firing of each GC.
source: Hence, functional heterogeneities among GC terminals also originate from the history of firing of each GC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies about activity-dependent modulation.

claim: The synaptic behavior of individual GC bouton may be tuned by an intermingled combination of factors including expression of Syn II, presynaptic receptor composition, presynaptic Ca2+ dynamic, number of active release sites, retrograde signaling and history of firing.
source: To summarize, the synaptic behavior of individual GC bouton may be tuned by an intermingled combination of factors including expression of Syn II, presynaptic receptor composition, presynaptic Ca2+ dynamic, number of active release sites, retrograde signaling and history of firing.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the various factors discussed that could contribute to synaptic diversity.

claim: At GC synapses, releasable synaptic vesicles are segregated in two pools: one with fully releasable vesicles and a second one with reluctant vesicles.
source: At GC synapses, releasable synaptic vesicles are segregated in two pools, one with fully releasable vesicles and a second one with reluctant vesicles, which are differentially poised for exocytosis (Doussau et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The fully-releasable pool supports glutamate release during single action potentials.
source: The fully-releasable pool supports glutamate release during single action potentials while the reluctant pool is recruited only by stimuli elicited at high frequencies (Doussau et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The reluctant pool is recruited only by stimuli elicited at high frequencies.
source: The fully-releasable pool supports glutamate release during single action potentials while the reluctant pool is recruited only by stimuli elicited at high frequencies (Doussau et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In Syn II KO mice, synaptic transmission is characterized by a defect in glutamate release by single action potentials and by a rapid recovery of synaptic transmission by 100 Hz stimuli.
source: In Syn II KO mice, synaptic transmission is characterized by a defect in glutamate release by single action potentials and by a rapid recovery of synaptic transmission by 100 Hz stimuli.
evidence: This is an observation based on the experimental data from Syn II KO mice.

claim: A lack of Syn II impairs pr of fully-releasable vesicles without affecting the recruitment of reluctant vesicles.
source: This suggests that a lack of Syn II impair pr of fully-releasable vesicles without affecting the recruitment of reluctant vesicles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations in Syn II KO mice.

claim: Syn II may act with several partners to control the recruitment of fully-releasable vesicles.
source: Potentially, Syn II may act with several partners to control the recruitment of fully-releasable vesicles.
evidence: This is speculation about the molecular mechanism of Syn II function.

claim: In GC terminals, Munc13-3 has been involved in superpriming steps that tightly couple synaptic vesicles with P/Q-type Ca2+ calcium channels or maturate the fusion machinery.
source: In GC terminals, Munc13-3 has been involved in superpriming steps that tightly couple synaptic vesicles with P/Q-type Ca2+ calcium channels (positional superpriming) or maturate the fusion machinery (molecular superpriming) (Ishiyama et al., 2014; Kusch et al., 2018; Schmidt et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Munc13-3 may indirectly act with Rab3-interacting molecules (RIMs) which are organizers of calcium channel and synaptic vesicles in the active zone.
source: Munc13-3 may indirectly act with Rab3-interacting molecules (RIMs) which are well known organizers of calcium channel and synaptic vesicles in the active zone (Südhof, 2013).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation about RIM function.

claim: Syn II interacts with both Rab3 and P/Q type calcium channels.
source: Since Syn II interacts with both Rab3 (Giovedì et al., 2004) and P/Q type calcium channels (Medrihan et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Munc13-3, Syn II, Rab3 and RIM may act in concert to reduce the physical distance between fully-releasable vesicles and Ca2+ channels.
source: it cannot be excluded that Munc13-3, Syn II, Rab3 and RIM act in concert to reduce the physical distance between fully-releasable vesicles and Ca2+ channels.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible molecular mechanism.

claim: Syn II-Rab3-RIM complex may directly regulate the influx of Ca2+ through strong inhibition of voltage-dependent inactivation of P/Q type Ca2+-channels.
source: Alternatively, Syn II-Rab3-RIM complex may directly regulate the influx of Ca2+ through strong inhibition of voltage-dependent inactivation of P/Q type Ca2+-channels (Hirano et al., 2017; Kintscher et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: Single GCs receive a combination of MF inputs coding for different modalities.
source: At the input stage of the cerebellar cortex, single GCs receive a combination of MF inputs coding for different modalities (Arenz et al., 2008; Chadderton et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The diversity of STP profiles across MFs from different origins provide temporal signatures for each combination of MFs converging on a single GC thus enhancing pattern decorrelation of sensory inputs.
source: The diversity of STP profiles across MFs from different origins provide temporal signatures for each combination of MFs converging on a single GC thus enhancing pattern decorrelation of sensory inputs (Chabrol et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Temporal coding in GCs is extended in the FFI pathway by an input-specific control of first-spike latency in MLIs.
source: Here, we show that temporal coding in GCs is later extended in the FFI pathway by an input-specific control of first-spike latency in MLIs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The combination of heterogeneous presynaptic behaviors at the successive stages of cerebellar computation leading to consecutive temporal signatures should refine the salient feature of a given combination of MF inputs.
source: The combination of heterogeneous presynaptic behaviors at the successive stages of cerebellar computation leading to consecutive temporal signatures, should refine the salient feature of a given combination of MF inputs and ultimately should enhances the representation of sensory information by PCs.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Synapse-specific temporal coding may have essential consequences for learning and predictive functions in the cerebellum.
source: Considering the importance of delay coding for internal models of motor adjustments (Kennedy et al., 2014; Kistler et al., 2000; Mauk and Buonomano, 2004; Wolpert et al., 1998) synapse-specific temporal coding may have essential consequences for learning and predictive functions in the cerebellum.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance, supported by citations.

claim: Long-term potentiation (LTP) of GC-PC connections require the coincidence of strong PF and MLI activities onto the same PC.
source: Indeed, long-term potentiation (LTP) of GC-PC connections require the coincidence of strong PF and MLI activities onto the same PC (Binda et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Induction of associative GC-MLI LTP may depend on the time window separating excitatory and inhibitory inputs onto PCs.
source: As exemplified by the rules governing the induction of associative GC-PC long-term depression triggered by coincident PF and climbing fiber activation (Suvrathan et al., 2016), induction of associative GC-MLI LTP may depend on the time window separating excitatory and inhibitory inputs onto PCs.
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to another form of plasticity, supported by a citation.

claim: Heterogeneous profiles of STP at MF-GC synapses and GC-MLI synapses induce wide range of delays between the direct excitatory pathway and FFI at the level of PC synapses.
source: Heterogeneous profiles of STP at MF-GC synapses and GC-MLI synapses necessarily induce wide range of delays between the direct excitatory pathway and FFI at the level of PC synapses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and knowledge of cerebellar circuitry.

claim: The fine tuning of STP at the level of single cells may have fundamental importance for the induction of long-term plasticity and ultimately for motor learning.
source: Hence, the fine tuning of STP at the level of single cells may have fundamental importance for the induction of long-term plasticity and ultimately for motor learning.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of the findings.
